name: Spellbook (Rust Hunspell-format spellchecker, rewrite of Nuspell)
workload: Criterion median time to check one word against the stock en_US dictionary for ten word shapes (in-dictionary, number, prefix and suffix stripping, title and upper case, hyphen breaks, compound), plus a Valgrind DHAT heap total for checking one word.
claimed_speedup: check(): 'earth' 42.82 ns vs Hunspell 197.25 ns and Nuspell 125.89 ns; '8675,309.0' 14.14 ns vs 220.89 and 112.92 ns; 'light-weight-like' 779.06 ns vs 4,329.10 and 1,248.90 ns; 'unearthed' 264.98 ns vs 405.81 and 521.53 ns. Not faster on every row: compound word '20000th' 676.08 ns vs Nuspell 656.35 ns (Hunspell 3,204.10 ns). DHAT total allocation for one check: Spellbook 2,580,386 bytes in 44,741 blocks vs Nuspell 4,437,599 bytes in 50,419 blocks and Hunspell 3,325,493 bytes in 90,736 blocks.
compiler_and_flags: Spellbook: cargo bench with Criterion (benches/check.rs). Hunspell and Nuspell: vendored C++ sources built through the cc crate in the-mikedavis/ffi-dictionaries and timed with nightly libtest #[bench]. No compiler versions, optimisation levels or flags are stated.
tradeoffs: Only check() is benchmarked; the author says dictionary load and suggestion matter less and does not measure them. Hunspell-format dictionaries. Rust crate; the repo ships no benchmark of its own against Hunspell, the C++ numbers come from a separate FFI harness.
caveats: First-party numbers, CPU and compiler not stated, so tier C. The two sides use different harnesses (Criterion vs nightly libtest, C++ called through FFI with c"word" literals). The word_with_suffix row is not apples to apples: the table lists 'earthed' but the ffi-dictionaries benches check 'earthly' (a literal stem in the dictionary, which skips suffix stripping) while Spellbook's check.rs now benches 'earthed' with a comment about that difference; the table row does not match the current benchmark sources. Spellbook is described as mainly a rewrite of Nuspell, so the win is implementation detail, not a new algorithm. The ffi-dictionaries harness is GPL-3.0. Only the en_US dictionary is in the table.
found_via: GitHub: helix-editor/spellbook README (Rust rewrite of Nuspell) links docs/compare.md; WebSearch 'Rust rewrite of C++ library faster than Nuspell OR hunspell...' returned the crate.
why_faster: Per the author: Spellbook uses hashbrown (SIMD group probing) with foldhash for the stem table where Nuspell rolls its own hash table with std::hash; Rust's standard library string search and equality are well optimised; small-string and small-slice optimisations cut memory. The author labels the string-search point a suspicion and does not profile it.

name: wc in Haskell ('Beating C with 80 lines of Haskell')
baseline: wc (the C wc shipped with the author's macOS; also wc -mwl for UTF-8)
workload: Wall-clock time to count bytes, lines and words of a 543 MB plain-text file (and 90 MB for single-core runs); UTF-8 mode compared with wc -mwl.
claimed_speedup: 543 MB plain: wc 2.07 s vs multicore Haskell 1.23 s and streaming Haskell 1.07 s (about 1.7x and 1.9x faster, derived from page data). UTF-8: wc -mwl 5.56 s vs multicore 3.07 s and streaming 2.67 s (about 2.1x, derived). Single-core Haskell does not win: 2.73 s vs wc 2.06 s on 543 MB, and 0.47 s vs 0.37 s on 90 MB.
compiler_and_flags: GHC; version and optimisation flags are not stated in the article.
tradeoffs: Peak memory on 543 MB: wc 1.87 MB, multicore Haskell 7.06 MB, streaming 17.81 MB (8.02 MB with 100 KB chunks). The parallel version splits one file by byte offsets.
caveats: Author calls the timings unscientific: averages after warming the disk cache, no confidence intervals. Baseline is the Mac's BSD-style C wc, not GNU wc, and its build flags are unknown. The Haskell win comes from using 4 cores against single-threaded wc and the author notes the parallel program uses more CPU time (4.22 s user). Single-core Haskell is slower than wc.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'Beating C wc word count Haskell OR Go OR OCaml OR Rust OR Zig github faster than GNU wc' and the 'Beating wc with C' write-up that links the Haskell, APL, Go and Futhark posts.
why_faster: Parallel (and streaming) chunked counting where each chunk yields a monoidal state that is merged across word boundaries; wc is single-threaded. No claim that Haskell code is faster per core.

name: wc.apl (Dyalog APL wc, 'Beating C with Dyalog APL')
baseline: wc (the C wc shipped with the author's macOS)
workload: Counting lines, words and bytes of a 1.661 GB text file, timed with a Dyalog timing operator (APL) against the time utility (wc).
claimed_speedup: APL wall time 3.36 s on the first run, then 2.75, 2.34 and 2.36 s (array-arithmetic version); windowed-reduction version 3.33 s first run then about 1.85 s; versus wc user times of 5.345 to 5.549 s. First naive APL attempt took 32.97 s.
compiler_and_flags: Dyalog APL interpreter (version not stated); wc build flags unknown.
hardware: 2.2 GHz Intel Core i7, 8 GB DDR3, 11-inch early-2015 MacBook Air
tradeoffs: Needs the Dyalog APL interpreter, which is proprietary (free for non-commercial use). Reads the file in 256 KB blocks and keeps word-boundary state between blocks.
caveats: The comparison mixes measurements: APL figures are wall-clock times from a timing operator while the wc figures are user CPU times from the time utility, and wc's wall time is not reported. Caches were warm after the first run. Single file, single machine, no variance. The README itself says faster wc versions likely exist.
found_via: GitHub: linked from the 'Beating wc with C' write-up (expr-fi/fastlwc) which cites the Haskell, APL, Go and Futhark posts.
why_faster: Array-oriented primitives over 256 KB blocks: boolean membership of whitespace, then a windowed reduction (2</) to count word starts; the README does not say whether the interpreter uses SIMD or several threads.

name: roxmltree (Rust read-only XML tree)
baseline: libxml2 (C) DOM parse, called through the rust-libxml wrapper
workload: Time to parse an XML document into an in-memory tree: tiny, medium (SVG), large (plist) and huge (XML) inputs from the repo's benches directory.
claimed_speedup: huge: roxmltree 2,997,887 ns vs libxml2 6,850,666 ns; large: 1,494,886 vs 3,250,606 ns; medium: 421,137 vs 950,984 ns; tiny: 2,522 vs 8,931 ns, i.e. about 2.2 to 3.5x faster (ratios derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench in the benches directory (bencher crate, libxml feature); rustc version and flags are not stated. libxml2 is the system library, version not stated.
tradeoffs: Read-only tree (no mutation); peak memory about 6 to 8 times the file size (1.1 GB sample peaks at 7.6 GB, 6.8 GB without the positions feature); forbids unsafe code; streaming quick-xml is slightly faster than roxmltree.
caveats: Own benchmark with partial methodology (CPU stated, compiler version and flags not), so tier C. The README itself says 'Since all libraries have a different XML support, benchmarking is a bit pointless'. libxml2 is driven through the rust-libxml wrapper, so FFI and wrapper costs are included, and libxml2 builds a feature-richer mutable tree. Only one machine (macOS arm64).
found_via: GitHub: crates.io scan of text and parser crates listed quick-xml; roxmltree README checked as an XML-parser lead and its Performance section compares against libxml2.
why_faster: README: names, comments and processing instructions are never allocated and nodes borrow from the input; the tree is read-only. The libxml2 side builds a full DOM; that contrast is this agent's inference, not stated by the author.

name: mojo-regex (Mojo regular expression library)
baseline: CPython 3.12 re module (C implementation) and the Rust regex crate
workload: 80 regex micro-benchmarks (literals, alternations, phone-number DFA patterns, is_match, findall) with pre-compiled patterns, 500 ms target runtime per case, median timing.
claimed_speedup: Mojo vs Python re: geomean 24.54x faster over 76 shared benchmarks (Mojo wins 74, Python wins 1). Mojo vs Rust regex: geomean 3.47x over 71 shared benchmarks (Mojo wins 59, Rust wins 11). Extreme rows such as is_match_digits 1.223 ns vs 9.300 us (7,607x) and is_match_predefined_word 1.176 ns vs 21.190 us (18,013x).
compiler_and_flags: Mojo 0.26.2 stable, default optimisation; CPython 3.12 re; Rust regex crate built --release with -C target-cpu=native.
tradeoffs: Missing features: named groups, case-insensitive matching, non-greedy quantifiers, word boundaries, Unicode character classes, multiline and dot-all modes, lookaround and negated shorthand classes (\S, \D, \W). Invalid patterns can fail the build when used with the compile-time API.
caveats: First-party, hardware not stated, so tier C; ratios above 50x (up to 18,013x) are implausible as engine speed and likely reflect Python call overhead on nanosecond rows and Mojo compile-time specialisation, so they cap the tier. Rows missing from one side are blank. The baseline is CPython's C sre engine, not PCRE2, RE2 or Hyperscan, and the Python timing includes interpreter call overhead.
found_via: GitHub: direct check of the msaelices/mojo-regex README ('Beats Python's C-based re module on 96% of benchmarks') after github.com/topics scans for regex engines in Zig and Go.
why_faster: Hybrid DFA, NFA, PikeVM and lazy-DFA engine chosen per pattern; an optional compile-time API builds the DFA in Mojo's comptime interpreter so matching needs no runtime compilation, pattern hashing or cache lookup (README).

name: sparkdown (Rust CommonMark parser)
workload: Render the 200 KB CommonMark spec fixture to HTML in process; cmark was also run command-line to command-line on a 16 MB Markdown document.
claimed_speedup: 0.59 ms for sparkdown vs about 1.9 ms for cmark (about 3.2x) on the 200 KB fixture; on the 16 MB document cmark took 3.2x sparkdown's wall time and 3.1x its retired instructions. The same table lists pulldown-cmark 0.68 ms and comrak 2.00 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Default zero-dependency Rust build; rustc version and profile not stated; cmark build flags not stated.
hardware: Apple Mac Studio (chip model not stated)
tradeoffs: Zero dependencies; 652 of 652 official CommonMark examples pass (README); opt-in GFM extensions; WebAssembly build about 1.6x slower than native.
caveats: First-party; the cmark figure is given as '~1.9 ms' and the in-repo cargo bench reproduces only the sparkdown versus pulldown-cmark pair, so the cmark number is not reproducible from the repo. In-process timing for Rust vs a process-level CLI run for cmark on the large file. Very new (v0.1.0, released 2026-06-27) with 3 stars. The README disputes rushdown's published pulldown-cmark figure (about 6 ms vs 0.67 ms measured), so the table is the author's own re-measurement.
found_via: GitHub: crates.io description scan for crates naming cmark ('byte-identical to cmark'); README Performance section.
why_faster: README: zero-copy source borrowing, SIMD byte-set matchers (simdjson-style nibble lookup) to skip plain text, a fused SIMD HTML escaper, an intrusive first-child/next-sibling node tree and reused scratch buffers. The block layer is a faithful port of cmark's incremental algorithm.

name: xmloxide (Rust reimplementation of libxml2)
baseline: libxml2 (C): XML parse, serialize and XPath
workload: Criterion comparison of parsing, serialization and XPath evaluation on five documents from 4.9 KB (Atom feed) to 374 KB, run with the system libxml2.
claimed_speedup: Serialization 1.5 to 2.4x faster (Maven POM 20.1 us vs 47.5 us; 374 KB document 614 us vs 1397 us). XPath //book[@id] 5.91 us vs 15.99 us (2.7x); count() 1.09 us vs 1.67 us (1.5x). Parsing is mostly not faster: SVG 6.3 KB 58.5 us vs 65.6 us (12% faster), but Atom, POM, XHTML and the 374 KB document are about 3 to 13% slower (374 KB: 2.15 ms vs 2.08 ms).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --features bench-libxml2 --bench comparison_bench against the system libxml2; rustc version, flags and libxml2 version not stated.
tradeoffs: Pure Rust with a C FFI header for embedding where libxml2 is used; README reports 119 of 119 libxml2 compatibility tests passing; arena tree.
caveats: First-party, hardware and flags not stated, so tier C. The headline is serialization and XPath; parsing (the usual workload) is slightly slower than libxml2 on four of five documents. Small inputs only (largest 374 KB). The README's statement that libxml2 became unmaintained in December 2025 is the author's.
found_via: GitHub: crates.io description scan for crates naming libxml2; README Performance section.
why_faster: README: arena-based tree makes serialization cheap; byte-level pre-checks, bulk text scanning, ASCII fast paths for names, zero-copy element name splitting, inline entity resolution, XPath '//' step fusion and name-test fast paths.
